tagline: A rainbow X-ray beam as fine as a virus maps how the crystals inside materials tilt and stretch, in 3D.
plainSummary: Metals, rocks and microchips are built from countless tiny crystals, or grains. How each grain is tilted, squeezed and stretched decides whether a turbine blade cracks or a transistor works, and 3DMN is a microscope for exactly that. Two curved, super-polished mirrors are designed to focus X-rays from the upgraded APS into a spot about 100 nanometres wide, roughly a thousand times thinner than a hair; a second station aims for 40 nanometres. The beam is a 'rainbow' of many X-ray colours, so every grain it passes through flashes a constellation of spots onto a camera half a metre above the sample; the pattern reveals how that grain is turned and distorted. A platinum wire about as thick as a hair, or a tiny gold barcode, then sweeps just above the surface. Watching which spots blink out tells a computer how deep each one came from, building the map in 3D. In October 2026 the station is in scientific commissioning: its first experiments began in the summer, and it is already listed for outside scientists' proposals.
expertSummary: 3DMN is the APS-U successor of the 34-ID-E polychromatic Laue microdiffraction / differential-aperture X-ray microscopy (DAXM) facility. It uses the outboard branch of the 1 mrad canted 34-ID straight: a 28 mm-period planar hybrid PM undulator (2.1 m, upstream slot, FDR) feeds a windowless canted-undulator front end (2 × 2 mm² exit mask at 25.4 m), a flat horizontally deflecting first mirror at 29.6 m (3.0 mrad, Si/Rh/Pt stripes, notched substrate against thermal bump) and a small-offset (~1.1 mm) horizontally deflecting Si(111) DCM at 53.8 m with pink-beam bypass; its second crystal is heated (ΔT ~ 60 K) so that silicon's thermal expansion tilts the mono exit beam onto the pink-beam focus. Two fixed-figure Pt-coated elliptical KB pairs at 3 mrad image the source onto a micro station (~60 m; ray-traced 103 × 68 nm², 4.9 × 10¹² ph/s/0.1%BW at 14 keV) and a nano station (~65.5 m; 37 × 37 nm², 4.9 × 10¹¹) - FDR Table 4.64 sizes are FWHM-like (the same ray traces give RMS ~50 × 35 nm and ~19 × 19 nm, FDR Fig. 4.61), requiring 0.4-0.75 nm rms figure error. The instrument keeps the 34-ID-E geometry: sample at 45°, area detector(s) in 90° reflection geometry ~0.5 m above the sample, a scanned Pt wire or Au coded aperture for depth resolution (~0.5-1 µm along the beam), monochromatic energy scans for absolute d-spacings and the dilatational strain, and a far-field detector for BCDI of Laue-indexed grains. 5.3-30 keV. Status 2026-10-05: scientific commissioning/early experiments; as-built focal sizes, detectors and the nano station are not yet documented publicly.

whatAPSUEnables.plain: The focused spot is a shrunken picture of the X-ray source. The upgraded ring makes that source about 19 times narrower from side to side and roughly 100 times brighter, so new, more precise mirrors can make a spot several times smaller and far more intense. Smaller spots let 3DMN look inside the tangled walls of defects that make metals strong, at single defects, at transistor-sized features and at specks squeezed to extreme pressure between diamond tips. More X-rays make 3D scans fast enough to follow a material while it is heated, loaded or switched, and the more coherent beam lets the micro station also make lens-free 3D images of a single grain it has just identified.
whatAPSUEnables.expert: Because KB optics image the source (spot ~ source FWHM × q/p, plus diffraction and figure-error terms), the 280 → 14.7 µm rms horizontal source reduction shrinks the geometric source image ~19× horizontally (vertical 10 → 3.2 µm, ~3×). Separately, state-of-the-art figured KB mirrors can be fully illuminated: the pre-upgrade differentially coated spherical KBs reached ~500 nm only when apertured to ~60 × 60 µm², and opening that aperture with better mirrors is the PDR's ~9× flux factor. Design ray traces give ~100 nm (micro) and ~40 nm (nano) FWHM-like sizes (RMS ~50 × 35 nm and ~19 × 19 nm, FDR Fig. 4.61) at full acceptance, with pink flux ~10¹⁴ ph/s and mono ~10¹¹–10¹² ph/s on sample. The PDR budget multiplies ×100 (MBA brightness) ×9 (fully illuminated state-of-the-art KBs) ×5 (coded-aperture/multi-edge depth scans) ×~10 (low-noise photon-counting detectors) for 900× to 45,000× gains, enabling: strain tensors inside individual dislocation-cell walls (~100 nm voxels), strain fields of single bulk dislocations (needs <100 nm), sub-200 nm mapping of additively manufactured dendrites, nano-DAC samples at terapascal pressures, and multi-reflection BCDI of grains pre-oriented by Laue. Greater horizontal coherence (coherent fraction at 14 keV rises from ~0.2% to ~9% horizontally by a Gaussian-source estimate) is what makes BCDI at the micro station practical.
quantitative: Horizontal electron source size 280 µm rms (pre-upgrade APS) → 14.7 µm rms (APS-U brightness mode, 324 bunches); vertical 10 → 3.2 µm rms

Source brightness up by a factor ~100; since the focus is an image of the source, focused spot size and intensity improve 'linearly with the brightness'. Caveat: this is the FDR's loose wording - for fixed optics the focused flux density scales with source brightness, while spot SIZE scales with source size × demagnification (not linearly with brightness). FDR Chapter 1 quotes a larger brightness gain (~540× at 20 keV for an ID optimised at 20 keV, Table 1.1); '~100' is the 3DMN section's round number
Focus: 300 nm × 300 nm (pre-upgrade web spec) or 300-500 nm (H) × 300-700 nm (V) (wiki) → design 103 × 68 nm² micro and 37 × 37 nm² nano at 14 keV (FWHM-like; RMS ~50 × 35 and ~19 × 19 nm)
Pink-beam flux on sample: ~10¹¹ ph/s pre-upgrade → ~10¹⁴ ph/s design; monochromatic ~10⁹ → ~10¹¹ (directory) to ~10¹² (PDR) ph/s
Old KBs reached ~500 nm only when apertured to ~60 × 60 µm²; fully illuminated new mirrors give ~9× more flux at the same or smaller spot
PDR overall gain estimate: ~900× for most experiments, ~4,500× for many, up to ~45,000× for some
Depth scans: coded aperture needs ~120 µm of scan (8 bits × 15 µm) vs a 600 µm wire scan with 1 µm steps - ~5× fewer frames, lower noise; PDR target 2000 → 400 images per depth scan
Projected raw data ~2.8 PB/year vs ~400 TB/year at pre-upgrade 34-ID-E

Estimated horizontal coherent fraction at 14 keV: ~0.2% (pre-upgrade) → ~9% (APS-U), using Gaussian source sizes/divergences from FDR Table 1.1 plus single-electron undulator terms for a 2.1 m device (derived here; treat as approximate)

techniques.name: Polychromatic (pink-beam) Laue micro/nano-diffraction
techniques.plain: A beam containing many X-ray colours hits the sample; every crystal grain picks out the colours it likes and reflects them as a pattern of spots. The spot pattern is a fingerprint of how the grain is turned and how its shape is distorted - no need to rotate the sample.
techniques.expert: Focused pink beam (~5-30 keV after mirror cutoff; most useful signal on the top detector is ~12-17 keV) with the sample fixed. Each spot gives a unit scattering vector q-hat but not |q| (harmonics nh,nk,nl overlap). Indexing (e.g. Chung & Ice 1999; LaueGo 'euler'; lauelab) yields the orientation matrix and the deviatoric strain tensor (5 components) from inter-spot angles, typically to ~10⁻⁴ (best cases ~2 × 10⁻⁵). Scanning the sample gives 2D orientation/strain maps; combined with DAXM gives 3D.

techniques.name: Differential-aperture X-ray microscopy (wire scan)
techniques.plain: Because the beam goes deep into the sample, spots from many depths land on the detector at once. A thin platinum wire is swept just above the surface; when its edge hides a spot, the line from detector pixel past the wire edge to the beam says exactly how deep that spot was made, much as a moving shadow tells you where a lamp is.
techniques.expert: Introduced by the ORNL group of Larson, Yang, Ice, Budai & Tischler (Nature 2002) in the APS microbeam programme that became 34-ID-E (the exact APS station used for the 2002 paper was not verified here). A Pt wire (historically ~50 µm; 100 µm / 101.5 µm in 2022-23 geometry files) is stepped (~1 µm) along H = (Y+Z)/√2, ~0.2-1 mm above the 45° sample. For each pixel, frame-to-frame intensity differences are assigned by triangulation (ray from pixel tangent to the leading or trailing wire edge intersected with the incident beam) to depth bins along the beam; trapezoid weighting accounts for finite pixel width (LaueGo/lauelab). A wire step dH along H moves the triangulated point along the beam by ~dH/√2 × L/(L-h) for a pixel directly above. Typical resolution 0.5-1 µm along the beam; pixel blur ~ pixel × (wire-to-beam distance)/(detector distance) ~0.1-0.4 µm for 200 µm pixels at ~0.51 m.

techniques.name: Coded-aperture depth-resolved Laue (mask scan)
techniques.plain: Instead of one wire, a tiny gold barcode slides over the diffracted beams. Each spot is blinked on and off in a unique on/off pattern, so a computer can decode where every signal came from using far fewer pictures.
techniques.expert: Gursoy, Sheyfer, Wojcik, Liu & Tischler (J. Appl. Cryst. 2022; RSI 2023; RSI 2025). 1D binary de Bruijn sequence of order 8, length 256 (every 8-bit window unique); bits 7.5 µm (Au) / 15 µm (open); ~4.6 µm electroplated Au on Si3N4 membrane, fabricated at Argonne CNM; placed ~0.84-1 mm above the sample and scanned in 1 µm steps. Decoding: exhaustive search for code offset p then non-negative least squares for the footprint s (d = A_p s), then ray tracing. Needs only ~8 bits (120 µm) of scan; digital autofocusing calibrates aperture pose (surge/sway/heave, yaw/pitch/roll) from a Si reference. The 3DMN computing plan names 'mask scan' reconstructions (R&D) as the expected default once algorithms mature.

techniques.name: Monochromatic energy-scan micro/nano-diffraction
techniques.plain: With the monochromator in, the beam is one pure colour. Scanning that colour through a spot tells its exact wavelength, which gives the true spacing of the atom layers - the one thing a rainbow pattern cannot tell you.
techniques.expert: Si(111) HDCM, dE/E ~ 10⁻⁴, 5.3-30 keV, switchable with the pink bypass at a fixed focal spot. Measuring the energy of one indexed reflection fixes the lattice scale, completing the full (6-component) strain tensor; energy scans with the wire give depth-resolved absolute d-spacings and 1D/3D q-space histograms ('3D k-space mapping'). Horizontal deflection of the horizontally polarized beam costs flux: the PDR's kinematic cos²(2θ) estimate gives ~1/2 loss at 5.3 keV, ~1/4 at 8 keV, ~10% at 12 keV; for perfect Si crystals the π-polarized Darwin width (and hence DCM throughput) scales as |cos 2θ|, i.e. ~28% / ~12% / ~5% loss (derived here). Diffraction to the top detector (vertical scattering plane, σ polarization) has no such loss.

techniques.name: Bragg coherent diffraction imaging on Laue-indexed grains
techniques.plain: Once the rainbow pattern has told scientists exactly how a tiny grain is oriented, they can switch to a single colour and record the speckled 'fuzz' around one spot far downstream. A computer turns that speckle into a 3D image of the grain's shape and internal strain.
techniques.expert: FDR lists BCDI as a third method at the micro station with a far-field detector; PDR places a movable small-pixel detector ~2-3 m from the sample (e.g. 75 µm pixels at 3.3 m for 1.5 µm particles at 12 keV), reaching reflections by energy scans with the sample fixed. Builds on the 34-ID-C Laue+BCDI workflow (Pateras et al. 2020) and on Laue-pre-oriented multi-reflection BCDI of FIB-extracted W (Hofmann et al.).

techniques.name: Scanning X-ray fluorescence
techniques.plain: Atoms hit by the beam glow with their own X-ray colours, so a side detector can map which chemical elements are where - handy for finding the exact spot to study.
techniques.expert: Energy-dispersive SDD (Vortex-class; PDR prefers 1 mm thick sensor for higher-energy lines) close to the sample for elemental maps and fiducial location; pre-upgrade 34-ID-E listed a Vortex SDD (directory) and a Ketek (wiki).

scienceCases.title: Hidden stresses inside dislocation cells of deformed metals
scienceCases.plain: When you bend copper, defects tangle into walls that divide each grain into cells. 3D Laue microscopy showed that cell walls and cell interiors push in opposite directions with surprisingly large and varied stresses. Smaller beams will see inside the walls themselves.
scienceCases.expert: Levine et al. (Nat. Mater. 2006) measured axial elastic strains in individual dislocation cells of deformed single-crystal Cu with depth-resolved submicron polychromatic beams at the APS (34-ID-E microbeam programme; station not stated in the abstract), reporting broad distributions of cell-to-cell elastic strain; follow-up work found cell interiors and walls with opposite-sign strains, consistent with Mughrabi's composite model. The APS-U case targets ~100 nm voxels to resolve strain within single cell walls; a 2026 study combined 0.5 µm DAXM at 34-ID-E (pre-upgrade data; one grain of polycrystalline 304L stainless steel after 2% tensile strain) with an unsupervised Cauchy-mixture ML model to segment subgrain/dislocation-cell structure and deviatoric strain (SharafEldin et al., Acta Mater. 303, 121624, 2026).

scienceCases.title: The strain field of a single dislocation
scienceCases.plain: A dislocation is a single misplaced row of atoms, but it bends the crystal around it. 3DMN aims to map that bending directly, deep inside a real material.
scienceCases.expert: Hofmann et al. (Nat. Commun. 2013) characterized lattice rotations and strains of one dislocation in a freestanding GaAs/In0.2Ga0.8As/GaAs membrane by Laue microdiffraction at 34-ID-E, matching anisotropic elasticity. Doing this for a dislocation in bulk material needs <100 nm beams - a stated APS-U driver for 3DMN.

scienceCases.title: Additively manufactured (3D-printed) alloys
scienceCases.plain: Metal 3D printing freezes molten metal in tree-like dendrites with chemistry changing every few hundred nanometres. 3DMN can map the full stress state at that scale.
scienceCases.expert: In IN625/718-type superalloys primary dendrite arm spacing is ~1 µm and secondary ~300 nm with matching solute segregation; pre-upgrade full-strain-tensor measurements at 34-ID-E averaged over this structure. A sub-200 nm probe plus energy scans resolves local full strain tensors.

scienceCases.title: Materials at terapascal pressure
scienceCases.plain: Squeezing hydrogen between diamond tips to millions of atmospheres leaves samples only a few micrometres wide. A 50 nm beam can pick out the sample from the diamonds around it.
scienceCases.expert: Nano-fabricated anvil tips limit samples to ~100 nm scales; the science case cites crystal structures of hydrogen phases III-V (1-3 µm samples) and diffraction at TPa pressures as needing ~50 nm beams with ~100× brightness. The long working distance of the micro station was chosen to accommodate cells and environments.

scienceCases.title: Strain engineering in transistors and oxide devices
scienceCases.plain: Chip makers deliberately stretch silicon to make electrons move faster. 3DMN can map that stretch inside finished devices, and watch domains switch in ferroelectric memories.
scienceCases.expert: Mapping strain in SOI/CMOS structures with <32 nm features, strain gradients at edges and interfaces, and ferroelectric/multiferroic nanodomains (stripe, toroidal, bubble) with in-situ fields and temperature; IBM's need for smaller probes is quoted in the PDR.

scienceCases.title: Find a grain, then image it coherently
scienceCases.plain: In a polycrystal you first need to know which grain to look at and how it is turned. The Laue pattern provides that map; then a single-colour coherent beam images the grain or a precipitate in 3D.
scienceCases.expert: PDR case for carbide precipitates at triple junctions in Inconel 617: index matrix grains by pink-beam Laue, predict a precipitate reflection's energy/direction, measure it coherently on a detector 2-3 m downstream. Related: Laue+BCDI at 34-ID-C (Pateras et al. 2020) and Laue-pre-oriented multi-reflection BCDI of FIB-extracted W containing chosen dislocations (Hofmann et al. 2020).

scienceCases.title: Coded apertures for fast 3D Laue
scienceCases.plain: Borrowing a trick from X-ray astronomy, scientists replaced the wire with a gold barcode so that 3D scans take a fraction of the time.
scienceCases.expert: Coded-aperture Laue on 75 µm Ni foil (7-30 keV pink, ~300 nm spot, PE detector 510.9 mm above the sample) recovered the full ~100 µm depth range with less noise than a 100 µm Pt wire scan using 5× fewer points; follow-ups added digital autofocusing and aperture-design rules (bit size ≥ signal size, aspect ratio ~1, ≥ 8-bit scan).

keyParameters.label: Energy range
keyParameters.note: FDR beam-delivery spec (shared with ATOMIC). Current APS Beamline Directory lists 5.5-30 keV; pre-upgrade 34-ID-E was 7-30 keV. Upper limit set by mirror critical angle; lower by mono geometry.

keyParameters.label: Source
keyParameters.value: Planar hybrid PM undulator, 28 mm period, 2.1 m, upstream slot of canted straight (outboard branch)
keyParameters.note: FDR Table 4.62. Max power 777 W through 2 × 2 mm² FE mask at 30 m with K = 2.459. As-built era: IPAC'24 (Dejus et al.) lists the new 2.8 cm canted HPMUs with required K = 2.48 at 8.5 mm minimum gap, E1 = 3.0 keV, canted length ~2.1 m.

keyParameters.label: Canting
keyParameters.value: 1 mrad between 3DMN (outboard/upstream) and ATOMIC (inboard/downstream)
keyParameters.note: 0.5 mrad canting magnets at both ends + 1 mrad magnet between the two undulators.

keyParameters.label: Front end
keyParameters.value: Canted-undulator front end (CUFE), windowless (differential pump), 2 × (2 mm H × 2 mm V) exit apertures 1 mrad apart at 25.4 m; 2 × 10 kW
keyParameters.note: Exit collimator 2 × (5 × 5 mm²) at 26.1 m.

keyParameters.label: First mirror (34ID-MR-1)
keyParameters.value: Flat, horizontally deflecting, 3.0 mrad, Si/Rh/Pt stripes, notched substrate, at 29.6 m
keyParameters.note: Absorbs up to ~189 W (Si stripe, 1 × 1 mm² acceptance, 9.1 keV 3rd harmonic), 0.48 W/mm² (FDR Table 4.66). PDR (2017) had proposed LN2-cooled Si mirrors. Deflection sense: FDR text does not state it, but the FDR Fig. 4.59 schematic (angles exaggerated) shows the 3DMN mirror steering its beam further outboard and the ATOMIC mirror steering inboard, as the PDR proposed.

keyParameters.label: Monochromator (34ID-MN-2)
keyParameters.value: Horizontally deflecting Si(111) double-crystal, ~1.1 mm offset, pink-beam bypass, heated 2nd crystal (ΔT ~ 60 K), at 53.8 m
keyParameters.note: Si(111) inferred from FDR Table 4.67 (12.5° at 9.1 keV) and stated in PDR. Acceptance needed < 300 × 300 µm². Pre-upgrade precursor: a new 1 mm-offset, horizontally reflecting Si(111) 'synthetic channel-cut' (6-20 keV, air-bearing granite stage, chamber slid sideways to switch pink/mono, heated 2nd crystal) was installed at 34-ID-C before the upgrade (Pateras et al. 2020).

keyParameters.label: Energy resolution (mono)
keyParameters.value: dE/E ~ 10⁻⁴
keyParameters.note: Si(111) double bounce; same as pre-upgrade spec.

keyParameters.label: Micro-focus spot (design, 14 keV)
keyParameters.value: 103 × 68 nm² (H × V) brightness mode; 91 × 100 nm² timing mode
keyParameters.note: ShadowOui ray trace, FDR Table 4.64; KB at ~60 m. Current Beamline Directory quotes 0.15 × 0.15 µm. No published as-built measurement found. Size definition is not stated in Table 4.64; the same ray traces give RMS ~50 (H) × 35 (V) nm at zero figure error (FDR Fig. 4.61), so the tabulated values are ~2× RMS, i.e. FWHM-like. APS-U Key Performance Parameters for feature beamlines were brightness at a defined energy plus usable energy range (only ISN had a focal-spot KPP), so 'all feature beamlines met their KPPs' (MEDSI 2025) does not certify a 3DMN spot size.

keyParameters.label: Nano-focus spot (design, 14 keV)
keyParameters.value: 37 × 37 nm² brightness mode; 38 × 37 nm² timing mode
keyParameters.note: KB at ~65.5 m. Whether the nano station is installed/commissioned as of Oct 2026 is not documented publicly. RMS ~19 × 19 nm in the same ray traces (FDR Fig. 4.61).

keyParameters.label: Flux on sample (design)
keyParameters.value: Micro 4.9 × 10¹², nano 4.9 × 10¹¹ ph/s/0.1%BW at 14 keV; pink ~10¹⁴ ph/s; mono ~10¹¹–10¹² ph/s
keyParameters.note: Pink/mono totals from PDR and Beamline Directory (10¹⁴ pink; 10¹¹ mono at 15 keV).

keyParameters.label: KB mirrors
keyParameters.value: Two fixed-figure (prefigured elliptical cylinder) Pt-coated KB pairs at 3.0 mrad; micro at ~60 m, nano at ~65.5 m
keyParameters.note: Figure-error tolerance (<10% spot growth): micro H 0.75 nm, V 0.5 nm rms; nano H 0.5 nm, V 0.4 nm rms.

keyParameters.label: Working distance
keyParameters.value: ≥ 50 mm (micro, design goal); ~30 mm (nano)
keyParameters.note: PDR 2017 values; PDR also gives focal lengths f_h = 70 mm, f_v = 142 mm (62 m station) and 55/120 mm (66 m station) - may differ as built.

keyParameters.label: Detector geometry (reference: pre-upgrade 34-ID-E)
keyParameters.value: PerkinElmer XRD1621 (2048 × 2048, 200 µm pixels, 409.6 mm square) ~511-513 mm above sample in 90° reflection geometry; two 1024 × 1024 (204.8 mm) PE side panels ~0.40 m perpendicular distance (~0.43 m to panel centre), outboard and inboard
keyParameters.note: From Gursoy et al. 2022 (510.9 mm), Das et al. 2018 ('XRD 1621', ~511 mm) and lauelab geometry files geoN_2022-03-29 / 2023-04-06 (top 'PE1621 723-3335', P_z ~513 mm; sides 'PE0822 883-4841/4843', P_z ~400 mm, |P| ~428 mm). Model naming is inconsistent across APS sources: the 2024 computing strategy lists 'PE XRD 1620 AN' + '2 × PE XRD 0820 AN', the 34-ID-E Instruments page lists XRD 0820 AN, while the 2022-23 geometry files identify the side panels as PE0822 units. 3DMN design calls for Pilatus-6M-class top detector + two 1-2M side detectors (computing strategy: Pilatus 6M + 2 × 2 MP, 6 → 10 Mpixel per point), but detector purchases were descoped from APS-U; as-built detectors unknown. A ModSim 2026 talk (Aug 2026) says 34-ID-E is planning a new detector with ~10× collection speed (model not stated; the same slides mention wire reconstructions 'with Eiger').

keyParameters.label: Sample geometry
keyParameters.value: Sample surface inclined 45° to the incident beam; wire moves along H = (Y+Z)/√2
keyParameters.note: 34-ID-E coordinates: X horizontal outboard, Y up, Z along beam; 45° reflection geometry.

keyParameters.label: Depth-resolving aperture
keyParameters.value: Pt wire (~50 µm historically; 100 µm in 2022 tests; 101.5 µm in geometry files) ~0.2-1 mm above sample; or Au coded aperture (4.6 µm Au, 7.5/15 µm bits, 256-bit de Bruijn)
keyParameters.note: ~50 µm Pt wire ~200 µm above surface on the 34-ID-E 'End near focus' photo page (CCD-era, pre-2009 setup); ~50 µm wire.

keyParameters.label: Depth resolution
keyParameters.value: ~0.5-1 µm along the beam (DAXM, pre-upgrade)
keyParameters.note: 0.5 µm in SharafEldin et al. 2026; 1 µm steps in coded-aperture work. Goal ~100 nm with the new beams, at ~5× more frames per scan unless coded apertures are used.

keyParameters.label: Strain resolution
keyParameters.value: ~10⁻⁴ in deviatoric strain (best ~2 × 10⁻⁵)
keyParameters.note: PDR: 'dd/d = 10⁻⁴'; 1999 APS report: better than 2 parts in 10⁵ under favourable conditions. Deviatoric tensor from white-beam indexing (Chung & Ice 1999); complete tensor by adding one monochromatic energy measurement (Ice et al. 2005). Geometry check (derived here): one 200 µm pixel at ~511 mm is ~3.9 × 10⁻⁴ rad in 2θ, i.e. ~2 × 10⁻⁴ in plane-normal direction / dd/d at 2θ = 90°, so the ~10⁻⁴ (best ~2 × 10⁻⁵) figures rely on sub-pixel peak fitting over many reflections (the PDR's '1 pixel ~ 10⁻⁴' design rule would need ~1 m detector distance).

keyParameters.label: Thermal stability requirement
keyParameters.value: Hutch 0.03-0.05 °C; nano-instrument enclosure ≤ 0.02 °C
keyParameters.note: A 100 mm Al part grows 100 nm for a 0.04 °C change (PDR).

keyParameters.label: Distances
keyParameters.value: Micro instrument 60.0 m, nano instrument 65.5 m, pink beam stop 66.9 m from source
keyParameters.note: FDR Table 4.63.

keyParameters.label: Analysis software
keyParameters.value: LaueGo (Igor Pro; wire-scan reconstruction, peak search, indexing 'euler', strain refinement) → lauelab (Python/C/CUDA, alpha, 2023-) and laue-portal (Dash web workflow, HPC/Polaris)
keyParameters.note: LaueGo by J. Z. Tischler; lauelab reproduces LaueGo arithmetic and supports wire-scan reconstruction and indexing; laue-portal; coded-aperture decoder 'cold'; 50 Polaris nodes processed 6-12 h coded-aperture scans (data from Feb/Apr 2023) and returned results 12-15 min behind the detector (SC'23 Workshops / XLOOP 2023 best paper). Background: Liu & Ice 2014 chapter.

insertionDevices.name: 3DMN undulator (U28, upstream)
insertionDevices.type: planar hybrid permanent-magnet undulator (new APS-U structure: NdFeB with heavy-rare-earth grain-boundary-diffusion coercivity enhancement, vanadium-permendur poles)
insertionDevices.notes: Upstream device of the canted 34-ID straight → outboard branch. K up to ~2.46 (value used for FDR max-power calc: 777 W through 2 × 2 mm² at 30 m); IPAC'24 lists required K = 2.48 at the 8.5 mm minimum gap, E1 = 3.0 keV. First harmonic E1 = 12.2/(1+K²/2) keV at 6 GeV → ~3.0 keV at K=2.459 (3rd harmonic 9.1 keV, FDR Table 4.66); higher energies via odd harmonics. APS-U HPMU drive: min gap 8.5 mm, gap taper up to 5 mm (useful to broaden the pink spectrum for Laue, as requested in the PDR). Note: ATOMIC's directory entry quotes 2.3 m for its revolver; the FDR value (2.1 m) is used here and is supported by IPAC'24 ('canted length ~2.1 m, full length ~2.4 m').

insertionDevices.name: ATOMIC undulator (revolver U25/U21, downstream) - partner beamline
insertionDevices.type: planar hybrid PM revolver undulator (two magnet arrays, 25 and 21 mm)
insertionDevices.notes: Downstream device → inboard branch feeding ATOMIC (34-ID-F). Max power 763/738 W through 2 × 2 mm² at 30 m (K = 1.939/1.305). Not part of 3DMN but shares the straight, canting magnets and front end.

source.canting: Two undulators canted by 1.0 mrad (0.5 mrad magnets at each end of the straight and a 1 mrad magnet between the devices). 3DMN = upstream device = outboard beam; ATOMIC = downstream device = inboard beam. Pre-upgrade (after the 2011 canting upgrade) the assignment was reversed: 34-ID-E took the INBOARD (downstream) beam and 34-ID-C the outboard beam.
source.frontEnd: Canted-undulator front end (CUFE) rated 2 × 10 kW and 280 kW/mrad², windowless exit with differential pumping, clearing magnet, low-power photon shutter, burn-through fixed mask, GRID fluorescence XBPM1 (+ XBPM2 integrated in the exit mask), photon and safety shutters; exit mask at 25.4 m with two 2 × 2 mm² apertures 1 mrad apart; W exit collimator 2 × (5 × 5 mm²) at 26.1 m.
source.sourceSizeAndDivergence: APS-U electron beam at the ID (FDR Table 1.1), brightness mode (324 bunches, 42 pm): σx = 14.7 µm, σy = 3.2 µm, σx' = 2.8 µrad, σy' = 1.3 µrad; timing mode (48 bunches, 32 pm): 12.9 / 8.8 µm, 2.5 / 3.7 µrad. Pre-upgrade APS: 280 / 10 µm, 11.6 / 3.4 µrad. Single-electron photon terms for a 2.1 m device at 14 keV (derived here, σr = √(2·λ·L)/(4·π), σr' = √(λ/(2L))): ~1.5 µm and ~4.6 µrad, giving total photon source ~14.8 × 3.6 µm rms and ~5.4 × 4.8 µrad rms. Caveat: the canted source points sit ~1 m either side of the straight centre where beta functions differ slightly.

branches.name: 3DMN (outboard canted branch)
branches.description: U28 (upstream undulator) → CUFE → outboard mirror MR-1 (34-ID-A) → masks (34-ID-B) → BPM, slits, small-offset HDCM with pink bypass, pink shutter (34-ID-C) → micro-diffraction instrument (~60 m) and nano-diffraction instrument (~65.5 m) in 34-ID-E → pink beam stop at 66.9 m.

branches.name: ATOMIC (inboard, partner)
branches.description: Context only (ATOMIC has its own exhibit). Revolver U25/U21 (downstream undulator) → inboard mirror MR-2 → ATOMIC DCM and zoom KB1 in 34-ID-C → shielded pipe straight through 34-ID-E (55.1-67.5 m) → KB2 and coherent-imaging diffractometer in 34-ID-F (~68-70 m) → beam stop 78.7 m.

components.name: 3DMN undulator (28 mm period, upstream)
components.distanceNote: Distances in this exhibit are measured, as in FDR Table 4.63, from the centre of the 34-ID straight (the canting-magnet position). The U28 is the UPSTREAM device; its centre is placed ~1.2 m upstream (approx.: two 2.1 m devices plus a central canting magnet in the ~4.8 m straight).
components.plain: The X-ray source: a 2.1-metre row of alternating magnets that makes the ring's electrons wiggle, so they shine an intense, narrow beam of X-rays down the beamline. Opening or closing the gap between the magnet rows tunes the X-ray colours.
components.expert: Planar HPMU, λ_u = 28 mm, L = 2.1 m, K ≤ ~2.46 (E1 ~3.0 keV at K = 2.459; 3rd harmonic 9.1 keV). 777 W through a 2 × 2 mm² aperture at 30 m. Drive allows up to 5 mm gap taper to broaden harmonics for pink-beam Laue.

components.name: Canting magnets (0.5 / 1.0 / 0.5 mrad)
components.distanceNote: Centre magnet at the straight centre (0 m, the distance reference); 0.5 mrad magnets at both ends of the straight (~±2.4 m, approx.).
components.plain: Three small steering magnets kink the electron path by just 0.06 degrees between the two undulators that share this straight section. Their two X-ray beams drift apart, so one source slot feeds two beamlines: 3DMN and its neighbour ATOMIC.
components.expert: 0.5 mrad magnets at both ends of the straight plus a 1 mrad magnet between the devices give a 1.0 mrad separation of the 3DMN (upstream/outboard) and ATOMIC (downstream/inboard) beams.

components.name: ATOMIC revolver undulator (U25/U21, downstream) - partner
components.distanceNote: Downstream device of the same straight, centre ~+1.2 m from the straight centre (approx.).
components.plain: The second undulator in the same straight section feeds ATOMIC, the sister beamline next door that images strain inside single nanocrystals. Its 'revolver' design carries two magnet rows to choose from.
components.expert: Revolver with 25 mm and 21 mm arrays, 2.1 m; 763/738 W through 2 × 2 mm² at 30 m.

components.name: Canted-undulator front end (CUFE)
components.distanceNote: Front end occupies roughly 14-25 m inside the tunnel/ratchet wall; 19.4 m is the documented position of the upstream (GRID) mask. Other element positions not given in FDR - approximate.
components.plain: The gatekeeper between accelerator and beamline. Inside the tunnel's concrete wall it can stop the beam in an instant, measures where the beam points and soaks up kilowatts of unwanted heat, all without a window that would spoil the beam's quality.
components.expert: Rated 2 × 10 kW and 280 kW/mrad²; clearing magnet, low-power photon shutter, burn-through fixed mask, GRID fluorescence XBPM1, photon shutter 2, safety shutters; windowless exit via differential pumping to preserve coherence.

specs.XBPM: GRID XBPM1 + XBPM2 in exit mask

components.name: Front-end exit mask (two 2 × 2 mm² apertures)
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.63.
components.plain: A heavy metal block with two 2-millimetre square holes, one for each twin beam. It lets only the bright core of each beam into the hutch and absorbs the rest.
components.expert: Standard canted exit mask: two 2(H) × 2(V) mm² apertures 1 mrad apart; XBPM2 integrated.

components.name: Front-end exit collimator
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.63.
components.plain: A tungsten block that stops stray high-energy 'braking radiation' (bremsstrahlung) from the accelerator that travels along with the X-rays.
components.expert: Tungsten, two 5 × 5 mm² apertures 1 mrad apart (narrowed to help beamlines with small-offset monochromators manage bremsstrahlung).

components.name: White-beam slits, inboard (ATOMIC) 34ID-SL-1
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.63.
components.plain: Adjustable tungsten-edged jaws that trim ATOMIC's beam, right beside 3DMN's own pair.
components.expert: CUFE variable-aperture photon absorber with W edge inserts (inboard).

components.name: White-beam slits, outboard (3DMN) 34ID-SL-2
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.63.
components.plain: Water-cooled jaws trim the raw 'white' beam to the central millimetre or so that 3DMN's optics need, removing heat before it reaches the mirror.
components.expert: Canted-undulator variable-aperture photon absorber with tungsten edge inserts. Downstream optics only need ~1 × 1 mm² at the mirror and <300 × 300 µm² at the mono.

components.name: Tungsten bremsstrahlung collimator 34ID-BC-1
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.63.
components.plain: A tungsten shielding block. It stops stray gamma rays from the accelerator so that only the X-ray beams continue.
components.expert: Tungsten collimator.

components.name: Lead bremsstrahlung collimator 34ID-BC-2
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.63.
components.plain: A lead block that adds a second layer of protection against stray high-energy radiation.
components.expert: Lead collimator.

components.name: Outboard horizontal deflecting mirror 34ID-MR-1 (3DMN)
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.63.
components.plain: 3DMN's first mirror: a super-flat silicon mirror struck at a grazing 0.17 degrees. It steers the 3DMN beam away from its twin and throws away the highest-energy X-rays and much of the heat. Three coating stripes act like gears for different energy ranges.
components.expert: Flat Si mirror, 3.0 mrad grazing (6 mrad deflection), horizontal; stripes bare Si / Rh / Pt selected by vertical translation for harmonic rejection (approx. critical-angle cutoffs at 3 mrad from electron density: Si ~10 keV, Rh ~22 keV, Pt ~28 keV - estimate here; PDR notes some usable flux up to 30 keV). Notched (side-cut) substrate reduces thermal deformation by ~10×; absorbed 189 W (Si) / 120 W (Rh) for 1 × 1 mm² acceptance; 0.1 µrad rms slope error assumed in ray traces. PDR states the 3DMN mirror deflects outboard and ATOMIC's inboard (~11 mrad between pink beams at 2.5 mrad grazing); the FDR text does not state directions, but the FDR Fig. 4.59 schematic shows the same opposite deflections (3DMN outboard).

specs.cooling: notch design (coolant not stated in FDR; PDR proposed LN2)

components.name: Secondary bremsstrahlung collimator 34ID-SC-1
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.63.
components.plain: Shielding just after the mirror. Now that the X-ray beam has been bent, anything still travelling straight ahead is unwanted radiation, and this block stops it.
components.expert: Secondary bremsstrahlung collimator downstream of MR-1.

components.name: Inboard horizontal deflecting mirror 34ID-MR-2 (ATOMIC)
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.63.
components.plain: ATOMIC's twin mirror, which steers the neighbouring beam the other way, toward the ring.
components.expert: Flat, 3.0 mrad, Si/Rh/Pt stripes, notch design; inboard deflection per PDR and FDR Fig. 4.59 schematic.

components.name: Secondary bremsstrahlung collimator 34ID-SC-2
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.63 (branch not stated).
components.plain: Another shielding block, stopping stray radiation that travels straight past the second mirror.
components.expert: Secondary bremsstrahlung collimator.

components.name: Diagnostic flag 34ID-BD-1
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.63.
components.plain: A fluorescent screen that can drop into the beams so a camera shows staff exactly where both beams are.
components.expert: Diagnostic flag for both pink beams.

components.name: Pink photon mask / white-beam stop 34ID-PM-1
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.63.
components.plain: The end of the 'white' beam. A heavy block stops anything still travelling straight, while two openings pass the mirror-reflected beams, now called 'pink' because the mirrors have filtered out the highest energies.
components.expert: Pink photon mask and white-beam stop at the end of the FOE.

components.name: Shielded transport A→B 34ID-ST-1
components.distanceNote: Spans 36.0-42.5 m (FDR Table 4.63; existing white-beam transport reused).
components.plain: A lead-shielded vacuum pipe carries both beams 6.5 metres across the experiment-hall floor to the next hutch, so people can walk around it safely.
components.expert: Existing WB shielded transport, 36.0-42.5 m.

components.name: Pink-beam photon mask, outboard 34ID-PM-3
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.63 (inboard PM-2 at same position for ATOMIC).
components.plain: A metal aperture that trims 3DMN's pink beam and protects everything downstream from a stray or misaligned beam.
components.expert: Pink-beam photon mask, outboard; the PDR described a septum mask here splitting the two beam paths into independent pipes.

components.name: Lead collimator / bremsstrahlung stop 34ID-BC-3
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.63.
components.plain: The last heavy lead shielding against stray high-energy radiation before the optics hutch.
components.expert: Pb collimator / bremsstrahlung stop.

components.name: ATOMIC double-crystal monochromator 34ID-MN-1
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.63 (ATOMIC BPM 49.7 m and slits 50.3 m precede it).
components.plain: ATOMIC's own crystal monochromator, a near-twin of 3DMN's, which picks out one X-ray colour for its coherent imaging.
components.expert: Small-offset HDCM, 5.3-30 keV, pink bypass, heated second crystal.

components.name: ATOMIC zoom KB1 34ID-MR-3
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.63 gives 52.0 m; FDR text says 'station C at 54 m' - conflict noted.
components.plain: The first of ATOMIC's two pairs of bendable focusing mirrors, which let it 'zoom' its spot size.
components.expert: Bendable KB pair (zoom 50 nm - 2 µm together with KB2 at ~68-69 m).

components.name: Beam position monitor, outboard 34ID-BD-3
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.63.
components.plain: A beam-position monitor that measures exactly where the 3DMN beam is. Keeping the beam steady matters, because any drift up here shows up at the 100-nanometre focus.
components.expert: Pink-beam BPM upstream of the 3DMN slits/mono; pointing stability matters because KB focus position scales with source/beam motion.

components.name: Slits (3D Nano) 34ID-SL-4
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.63.
components.plain: Precision jaws that choose how much of the beam travels on to the monochromator and the focusing mirrors.
components.expert: Beam-defining slits before the HDCM; acceptance at the mono needs only <300 × 300 µm² (PDR).

components.name: Small-offset horizontal double-crystal monochromator 34ID-MN-2 (3DMN)
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.63.
components.plain: Two silicon crystals that pick out one pure X-ray colour. They are designed to slide out of the way in a few seconds, letting the full rainbow through: the mode shown here. The second crystal is kept about 60 °C warmer so that the single-colour beam lands on the same spot of the sample as the rainbow.
components.expert: Si(111) HDCM, 5.3-30 keV (θ_B ~21.9° at 5.3 keV to ~3.8° at 30 keV), offset ~1.1 mm, pink-beam bypass; heater under crystal 2 (ΔT ~ 60 K) changes d by α·ΔT (α_Si ~2.6 × 10⁻⁶/K), tilting the exit beam by ~2·α·ΔT·tan(θ_B) (~125/70/45/21 µrad at 5.3/9/14/30 keV for ΔT = 60 K, derived here) so the mono beam is brought back onto the pink beam at the final focusing optics/sample (FDR; Pateras et al. 2020 say 'coincident to the pink beam in the final focusing optics'). Closing a full 1.1 mm offset at the micro KB (~6 m downstream) would need ~180 µrad, so the exact operating scheme (energy-dependent ΔT, residual offset) should be confirmed with staff. Requirements (PDR): 0.2 µrad rms rotational stability, collinear pink/mono exit, passes the neighbouring canted beam. Absorbs ~1-2 W (0.3 × 0.3 mm² acceptance). Successor of the 34-ID-E 'micro-monochromator' formerly in 34-ID-D. Pre-upgrade precursor: a 1 mm-offset horizontally reflecting Si(111) synthetic channel-cut with heated 2nd crystal, on an air-bearing granite stage that slides the crystals in/out of the pink beam, was installed at 34-ID-C (Pateras et al. 2020).

components.name: Pink-beam shutter, outboard 34ID-SH-2
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.63 (ATOMIC SH-1 at same position).
components.plain: A heavy safety shutter. When it closes, the 3DMN hutch is safe to enter, even while ATOMIC keeps running next door.
components.expert: Pink-beam photon/safety shutter for 34-ID-E access.

components.name: ATOMIC shielded transport through 34-ID-E 34ID-ST-2
components.distanceNote: Spans 55.1-67.5 m (FDR Table 4.63). In FDR Fig. 4.58 it runs ~0.4 m inboard of the 3DMN beam (approx. from figure).
components.plain: ATOMIC's beam passes straight through the 3DMN hutch inside a lead-shielded pipe, so both beamlines can work at the same time.
components.expert: Shielded pipe delivering the inboard pink beam to 34-ID-F; 3DMN users can enter E while ATOMIC runs.

components.name: Micro-focusing KB mirror pair (micro-diffraction instrument 34ID-BI-1)
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.63 / text: KB and instrument at 60 m (ray traces at '60 m'). Deflection field: the pair deflects both vertically (first mirror) and horizontally (second mirror).
components.plain: Two short curved mirrors, one squeezing the beam vertically and one sideways, focus it to about 100 nanometres. Unlike lenses, mirrors bend every X-ray colour the same way, so the rainbow and the single colour meet at exactly the same spot.
components.expert: Prefigured elliptical-cylinder Si mirrors, Pt coated, 3.0 mrad, non-dispersive; ray-traced 103 × 68 nm² (brightness mode, 14 keV; FWHM-like, RMS ~50 × 35 nm), 4.9 × 10¹² ph/s/0.1%BW; figure error <0.75 nm (H) / <0.5 nm (V) rms. PDR design: f_h ~70 mm, f_v ~142 mm, ≥50 mm working distance (focus also possible at larger WD with lower demagnification). Pair geometry: vertically focusing mirror upstream, horizontally focusing mirror closer to the focus (PDR focal lengths; same ordering as the old 34-ID-E pair in the CCD-era 'End near focus' photo: 90 mm mirror 130 mm from focus, 40 mm mirror 60 mm from focus); each deflects the beam by ~6 mrad (vertical and horizontal respectively; deflection senses not documented).

components.name: Micro station sample stage (45° geometry)
components.distanceNote: Approx.: focus ~0.1 m downstream of the 60.0 m KB position (PDR focal lengths f_v ~142 mm, f_h ~70 mm); not tabulated.
components.plain: The sample sits tilted at 45 degrees on a stack of motorised stages that step it through the focus in tiny moves, building a map point by point. A microscope looks squarely at its tilted face, and there is room around it for heaters, loading rigs or diamond pressure cells.
components.expert: xyz scanning stage with ~10 nm resolution, able to carry small samples and environmental cells (e.g. diamond-anvil cells); sample surface at 45° to the beam (34-ID-E X-Y-Z: X outboard, Y up, Z downstream). An optical microscope views the sample face-on, along F = (-Y+Z)/√2, i.e. along the surface normal.

components.name: Depth-profiling wire / knife-edge scanner (DAXM)
components.distanceNote: Approx.: at the micro sample; wire ~0.2-1 mm above the sample surface.
components.plain: A platinum wire about as thick as a hair glides just above the sample. Each time its edge hides a diffraction spot, simple geometry reveals how deep below the surface that spot was made, much as a moving shadow tells you where a lamp is. (Wire and gap are enlarged in the model so you can see them.)
components.expert: Pt wire (~50-100 µm diameter) on a scanning stage moving along H = (Y+Z)/√2 parallel to the sample surface; ~1 µm steps; leading/trailing edges both usable. PDR: <10 nm resolution, longer travel than the sample stage. Typical wire scan 50-2000 frames per sample point.

components.name: Coded aperture (gold barcode mask) - R&D option
components.distanceNote: Approx.: replaces the wire at the micro sample, ~0.84-1 mm above the surface (as in the 34-ID-E tests); drawn parked beside the wire.
components.plain: An experimental alternative to the wire: a tiny gold 'barcode' whose pattern never repeats. One short sweep encodes the depth of every spot at once, so a 3D scan needs a fraction of the pictures. (Shown parked beside the wire, enlarged.)
components.expert: 256-bit order-8 binary de Bruijn sequence, Au bars 7.5 µm (fabricated ~4.5 µm wider), gaps 15 µm, ~4.6 µm thick on Si3N4; scanned 1 µm steps; ≥ 120 µm scan for unique decoding; decoded by offset search + NNLS, pose by digital autofocusing.

components.name: Main area detector above the sample (90° reflection geometry)
components.distanceNote: Along-beam position = micro sample (60.1 m). Panel centre ~0.513 m above the sample and ~30 mm downstream of it, face horizontal (pre-upgrade lauelab geometry file geoN_2023-04-06; 510.9 mm in Gursoy et al. 2022).
components.plain: A large flat X-ray camera hangs half a metre above the sample, looking down. It catches the constellation of Laue spots thrown up at about 90 degrees, a fingerprint of each grain's tilt and strain. The coloured rays in the model are calculated for two nickel grains; their colour shows each spot's X-ray energy.
components.expert: Pre-upgrade: PerkinElmer XRD1621 a-Si flat panel (code-named 'Orange'; listed as 'XRD 1620 AN' in the 2024 computing strategy), 2048 × 2048, 200 µm pixels, 409.6 mm square, ~510.9-513 mm above sample, face horizontal, centre ~30 mm downstream of the sample (2023 geometry file). The PDR's design rule is 1 pixel ~ 10⁻⁴ in dd/d; at ~0.51 m one 200 µm pixel is ~2 × 10⁻⁴, so ~10⁻⁴ relies on sub-pixel peak fitting. 3DMN design: Pilatus-6M-class low-noise photon-counting detector (<200 Hz needed) - purchase descoped from APS-U; as-built model unknown.

components.name: Two side area detectors
components.distanceNote: Along-beam position ~ micro sample; panel centres ~0.14 m upstream of it. Each panel is tilted 45° about the beam axis (face normal pointing up-and-outboard / up-and-inboard), ~0.40 m perpendicular distance, centre ~0.43 m from the sample: 'Yellow' outboard, 'Purple' inboard (pre-upgrade lauelab geometry file geoN_2023-04-06).
components.plain: Two smaller cameras, tilted in from either side, catch spots the main camera misses. A wider spread of spots makes the measured tilt and distortion of each grain, especially its shear, more precise.
components.expert: Pre-upgrade: two PerkinElmer 1024 × 1024 a-Si panels (200 µm pixels, 204.8 mm square) code-named 'Yellow' (outboard) and 'Purple' (inboard); listed as XRD 0820 AN on the 34-ID-E Instruments page and in the 2024 computing strategy, but identified as 'PE0822' units in the 2022-23 lauelab geometry files; ~0.40 m perpendicular distance (~0.43 m to panel centre); each panel is tilted 45° about the beam axis with its centre ~0.14 m upstream of the sample, i.e. centred near 2θ ~ 110° at ~40-45° elevation (2023 geometry file). Design: two 1-2 Mpixel detectors (computing strategy: 2 × 2 MP). Larger solid angle improves off-diagonal strain components.

components.name: Fluorescence detector (SDD)
components.distanceNote: Along-beam position ~ micro sample; snout a few cm from the sample (approx.).
components.plain: Atoms struck by the beam glow with X-ray colours unique to each element. This detector reads that glow to map the chemistry and to find landmarks on the sample.
components.expert: Vortex-class SDD; 1 mm thick sensor preferred (PDR).

components.name: Far-field coherent (BCDI) detector, movable
components.distanceNote: Approx.: PDR places it ~2-3 m from the micro sample (e.g. 3.3 m at 12 keV for 1.5 µm particles with 75 µm pixels). Drawn ~2.2 m away, up and outboard (2θ ~72°, e.g. Ni 400 at 12 keV) so the diffracted ray leaves through the 45° sample surface and clears the gantry and side detectors; its along-beam coordinate is therefore ~60.8 m. Position illustrative.
components.plain: A camera placed metres away records the fine speckle around a single diffraction spot. A computer turns that speckle into a 3D image of one grain's shape and inner strain, coherent imaging made practical by the upgraded source.
components.expert: Small-pixel detector on a robot or large x-y translator to intercept one Bragg reflection; energy scans move through the rocking curve with the sample fixed. Micro station only (FDR).

components.name: Nano-diffraction thermal enclosure
components.distanceNote: Approx.: upstream wall of a ~2.8-3 m enclosure around the 65.5 m instrument (3000 mm dimension in FDR Fig. 4.67; ~2.5 m footprint at ~64.3-66.8 m in Fig. 4.58).
components.plain: The nano station is designed to sit in its own clear-walled room inside the hutch. A change of a few hundredths of a degree would make its parts grow by more than the beam is wide, so this enclosure is meant to hold the air steady to 0.02 °C.
components.expert: Separate temperature control to ≤ 0.02 °C (hutch 0.03-0.05 °C); electronics moved outside; granite/ultra-stable table (old steel-leg table gave ~50 nm rms vibration).

components.name: Nano-focusing KB mirror pair (nano-diffraction instrument 34ID-BI-2)
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.63 / text: 65.5 m (ray traces at '65 m'). Deflection field: the pair deflects both vertically (first mirror) and horizontally (second mirror).
components.plain: A shorter-focus mirror pair, further from the source, designed to squeeze the beam to about 40 nanometres, small enough to probe single defects in a crystal.
components.expert: Prefigured elliptical, Pt coated, 3.0 mrad; ray-traced 37 × 37 nm² (FWHM-like; RMS ~19 × 19 nm), 4.9 × 10¹¹ ph/s/0.1%BW at 14 keV; figure error <0.5 nm (H) / <0.4 nm (V) rms; PDR: f_h ~55 mm, f_v ~120 mm, ~30 mm working distance, slope error ~0.05 µrad.

components.name: Nano station sample stage with interferometric nanopositioners
components.distanceNote: Approx.: a few cm downstream of the nano KB.
components.plain: An ultra-precise stage, tracked by laser interferometers, holds the sample steady to a few nanometres while it is scanned.
components.expert: Interferometric nano-positioners on an ultra-stability optical table (FDR Fig. 4.67); PDR: xyz stage and knife-edge with ~5 nm precision.

components.name: Nano station precision knife-edge / wire scanner
components.distanceNote: Approx.: just above the sample.
components.plain: The nano station's depth-finding wire, moved with nanometre precision: the same moving-shadow trick at a finer scale.
components.expert: Precision knife-edge scanner (FDR Fig. 4.67), ~5 nm precision (PDR); same DAXM / coded-aperture principle.

components.name: Nano station flat-panel detectors
components.distanceNote: Above/around the sample (approx.).
components.plain: X-ray cameras around the nano sample collect its Laue patterns. The probed volume is tiny and its signal faint, so they must be very low-noise.
components.expert: 'Multiple near-field area detectors' (FDR); design: one large low-noise detector above plus two at the sides and a forward-scattering detector; as-built unknown.

components.name: Pink-beam stop, outboard 34ID-BS-1
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.63; end of the 3DMN beam.
components.plain: The end of the line: a block of heavy metal that safely absorbs whatever beam is left.
components.expert: Pink beam stop for the outboard branch at the E/F wall.

components.name: ATOMIC coherent-imaging endstation (34ID-BI-3) - partner
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.63 (KB2 at 68.1 m; beam stop 78.7 m).
components.plain: Next door in 34-ID-F, ATOMIC uses the twin beam for coherent imaging of strain inside individual nanocrystals.
components.expert: Sample and detector diffractometers, zoom KB2 at 68.1 m, 5.3-30 keV; listed for context only.

enclosures.name: 34-ID-A
enclosures.role: First optics enclosure (FOE), white beam; shared by 3DMN and ATOMIC
enclosures.notes: Boundaries read from the FDR Fig. 4.58 scale bar (± ~0.3 m; width very approximate). Contains FE exit mask/collimator, both CUFE white-beam slits, W and Pb collimators, both horizontal deflecting mirrors (29.6 m, 31.3 m), secondary collimators, diagnostic flag and the pink mask / white-beam stop (34.0 m). Downstream of PM-1 only pink beam exists.

enclosures.name: 34-ID-B
enclosures.notes: Approx. from Fig. 4.58. Reached via shielded transport 36.0-42.5 m. Houses inboard/outboard pink photon masks (46.9 m) and Pb collimator/bremsstrahlung stop (47.3 m).

enclosures.name: 34-ID-C
enclosures.role: Optics enclosure for both branches (repurposed former 34-ID-C coherent-diffraction station)
enclosures.notes: Approx. from Fig. 4.58. ATOMIC BPM/slits/DCM/KB1 (49.7-52.0 m), 3DMN BPM (52.7), slits (53.1), HDCM (53.8) and both pink-beam shutters (54.8 m) at its downstream wall. Downstream wall placed at ~55.0 m: FDR Table 4.63 puts the pink-beam shutters (inside C) at 54.8 m and the start of the 'shielded pipe through 34-ID-E' at 55.1 m.

enclosures.name: 34-ID-E
enclosures.role: 3DMN experimental station (micro- and nano-diffraction instruments); ATOMIC transport passes through
enclosures.notes: Approx. from Fig. 4.58/4.68: stepped outline, ~2.6 m wide from ~55.0 to ~59.3 m (footprint of the old 34-ID-D third optics enclosure) and ~4.3 m wide from ~59.3 to 67.5 m. PDR (2017) planned to join the old D and E stations and add ~2 m. Instrument footprints drawn at ~58.2-60.7 m (micro) and ~64.3-66.8 m (nano). Requires 0.03-0.05 °C air stability and a temperature-stabilized user/control area at the entrance (PDR). Upstream wall ~55.0 m constrained by FDR Table 4.63 (shutters 54.8 m in C; ST-2 'through 34-ID-E' 55.1-67.5 m). The FDR's instrument ESD is titled '34-ID-D/E 3DMN Endstation Instrumentation', consistent with D and E having been merged.

enclosures.name: 34-ID-F

instruments.name: 3D micro-diffraction instrument (34ID-BI-1)
instruments.plain: The workhorse station: a mirror pair focuses rainbow or single-colour X-rays to about 100 nm on a sample tilted at 45 degrees. A wire or gold barcode sweeps above it for depth, cameras above and beside it catch the Laue spots, and a far camera can do coherent imaging. Room is left around the sample for heaters, loading rigs or pressure cells.
instruments.expert: Base table and stabilisation structure, sample and knife-edge (wire) scanning stages, final KB optics (FDR 103 × 68 nm² at 14 keV; directory quotes 150 × 150 nm), multiple near-field area detectors and a far-field BCDI detector. Four operating modes shared with the nano station: pink micro, mono micro, pink nano, mono nano; three methods: polychromatic, monochromatic, BCDI (micro only). Workflow: wire/mask y-scans of 50-2000 frames per point → depth reconstruction → peak search/indexing → orientation/strain, plus energy scans for absolute strain.
detectors: Large area detector above sample, 90° reflection geometry (pre-upgrade PE XRD1621 2048² at ~511 mm; design Pilatus 6M class)
Two side area detectors (pre-upgrade PE 1024² panels, XRD 0820 AN / 'PE0822'; design 1-2 Mpixel)
Forward-scattering medium area detector on horizontal motion (PDR); pre-upgrade directory lists a Mar 165 CCD for forward scattering
Movable far-field small-pixel detector ~2-3 m for BCDI
sampleEnvironments: Small environmental chambers within ≥ 50 mm working distance (PDR)
Heating/cooling, electric/magnetic fields and mechanical loading (FDR science scope)

instruments.name: 3D nano-diffraction instrument (34ID-BI-2)
instruments.plain: A quieter twin at the back of the hutch, designed to focus to about 40 nm for the finest details. It is meant to sit in its own clear-walled room, held steady to two-hundredths of a degree. Its public status in 2026 is not documented.
instruments.expert: Ultra-stable optical table, thermal enclosure (≤ 0.02 °C), nanoscale sample and knife-edge stages with interferometric nanopositioners (~5 nm), short-focus KB (37 × 37 nm² design), multiple near-field flat-panel detectors (very low noise required since diffracted signal scales with depth-voxel length). Public confirmation of its as-built/commissioned state was not found (Oct 2026).
detectors: Flat-panel / photon-counting area detectors above and beside the sample (design)
sampleEnvironments: Reduced working distance (~30 mm, PDR) limits environments to compact stages

geometryNotes: Canted pair: 3DMN is the UPSTREAM undulator of the 34-ID straight and the OUTBOARD beam; ATOMIC is downstream/inboard, 1 mrad apart (FDR). This reverses the pre-upgrade assignment (old 34-ID-E used the inboard beam). Each branch has its own flat mirror in 34-ID-A at 3.0 mrad grazing (6 mrad deflection) - 3DMN at 29.6 m, ATOMIC at 31.3 m; the PDR states the 3DMN mirror deflects outboard and ATOMIC's inboard (~11 mrad between pink beams at 2.5 mrad), and the FDR Fig. 4.59 schematic shows the same; in FDR Fig. 4.58 the 3DMN pink beam runs ~0.4 m outboard of the ATOMIC shielded pipe through 34-ID-E (approx. from the drawing; consistent with opposite deflections: ~58 mm from canting + ~6 mrad × 28 m on each side). Both monochromators are horizontally deflecting small-offset (~1.1 mm) DCMs in 34-ID-C, so the mono beam is offset sideways by ~1 mm, not up. All hutches are on the experiment floor in the existing sector-34 footprint (no long-beamline building): A (FOE) ~24.4-36.0 m, shielded transport 36.0-42.5 m, B ~42.3-47.8 m, C ~47.8-55.0 m, E ~55.0-67.5 m (stepped width), F ~67.5-79.8 m (approx. from FDR figure scale bar). Inside E the 3DMN beam ends at a pink beam stop at 66.9 m while ATOMIC's beam continues in a shielded pipe (55.1-67.5 m) into F. Instrument geometry to reproduce: beam along +Z; sample surface tilted 45° (normal pointing up-and-upstream); the main detector looks straight down on the sample from ~0.5 m above (2θ ~ 90° at its centre), two side detectors at ~0.4 m (perpendicular; ~0.43 m to centre) outboard/inboard and slightly upstream/up; wire moves along H = (Y+Z)/√2, i.e. parallel to the sample surface, ~0.2-1 mm above it; KB pair just upstream of the sample (V mirror first, H mirror ~6-7 cm from focus for the micro station per PDR focal lengths). 34-ID-E coordinates: X horizontal outboard (toward the hutch doors), Y up, Z downstream. The nano instrument sits inside a ~3 m long glass thermal enclosure on an ultra-stable table at the downstream end of E. Exhibit conventions: distances are measured from the centre of the 34-ID straight (U28 centre at ~-1.2 m, ATOMIC revolver at ~+1.2 m); hutch outlines and offsets are read from FDR Fig. 4.58; the 1 mrad canting plus opposite 6 mrad mirror deflections put the two beams ~0.4 m apart in 34-ID-E. Sub-millimetre parts (wire, coded aperture, sample gap, DCM crystal offset) are enlarged in the 3D model for visibility; their true sizes are in the text.

interactiveIdeas.title: Laue constellation: rainbow vs. one colour
interactiveIdeas.concept: Visitor rotates a crystal (e.g. fcc Ni) under a focused beam. Pink mode: a constellation of spots appears on a detector panel 0.5 m above. Mono mode: almost all spots vanish; an energy slider scans until one spot lights up, revealing its exact energy.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: Why polychromatic Laue sees every grain without rotating the sample, why spot positions give orientation, and why a single-colour energy scan is needed to get the absolute lattice spacing.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: Bragg: λ = 2 d sin(θ); E[keV] = 12.398/λ[Å]. k_out = k_in - 2(k_in·n)n for plane normal n; a spot exists if the required energy E_hkl = 12.398/(2 d_hkl sin θ) lies in the incident band (~5-30 keV after the mirror; most signal 12-17 keV on the top detector). Harmonics (nh nk nl) land on the same pixel. Top detector centre at 2θ = 90°, so E = 12.398/(√2 d). Spot intensity ~ |F_hkl|² × spectrum × Lorentz/polarization; undulator harmonics (U28 E1 = 12.2/(1+K²/2) keV) make the 'rainbow' lumpy unless tapered.

interactiveIdeas.title: The wire that sees depth (DAXM)
interactiveIdeas.concept: Side view: beam enters a 45° sample; three grains at different depths send rays up to a pixelated detector. Visitor drags a wire across; per-pixel intensity curves step down; taking the difference and tracing the ray past the wire edge places each signal at its depth, building a 3D grain map.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: Depth resolution comes from geometry (pinhole-camera triangulation), not from focusing; why many frames are needed and what limits resolution.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: Depth along beam D = intersection of the line (pixel → tangent point on wire edge) with the beam line (lauelab formulas: tan(φ) = (tan φ0 ∓ tan dφ)/(1 ± tan φ0 tan dφ), tan dφ = a/√(r² - a²)). For a pixel directly above the wire, a wire step dH along H = (Y+Z)/√2 moves the triangulated point along the beam by dH/√2 × L/(L-h) ~ 0.71 dH (h = wire height ~0.2-1 mm, L ~ 510 mm). Pixel blur ~ p·h/L ~ 0.08-0.4 µm for 200 µm pixels. Depth below surface = depth along beam × sin(45°). Leading edge removes intensity (positive difference), trailing edge restores it (negative). Wire diameter 50-100 µm Pt; step ~1 µm; scan length set by the angular fan (hundreds of µm).

interactiveIdeas.title: Barcode for X-rays (coded aperture)
interactiveIdeas.concept: Replace the wire with a gold barcode built from a de Bruijn sequence. Each pixel records an on/off 'Morse code'; the visitor slides a window along the code to find the unique match and thus the depth. A race: wire scan vs. barcode scan to reconstruct the same grain map.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: How x-ray-astronomy coded apertures were miniaturised to speed up 3D microscopy; uniqueness of every 8-bit window; trade-off between bit size, thickness and noise.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: Order-8 binary de Bruijn sequence, length 256 (every 8-bit substring unique); bits 7.5 µm (Au, 1) / 15 µm (open, 0) → ≥ 120 µm scan for unique decoding vs ~600 µm wire scan; measurement d = A_p s (Toeplitz coding matrix); decode by exhaustive offset search + NNLS; 4.6 µm Au transmits a significant fraction at 20-30 keV (contrast drops with energy and with obliquity up to ~20° on a 51 cm detector); signals larger than a bit blur the code.

interactiveIdeas.title: Shrink the source, shrink the spot
interactiveIdeas.concept: Split screen: old APS vs APS-U source shapes (280 × 10 µm vs 14.7 × 3.2 µm rms) feed the same KB pair. Sliders for mirror distance/focal length, slit opening and mirror figure error show spot size and flux.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: A focused spot is an image of the source; brightness, not just flux, sets how small and intense the spot can be; why the old station had to throw away photons with slits and why sub-nanometre mirror figure is needed.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: Spot FWHM ~ √[(2.355 σ_src q/p)² + (diffraction ~ 0.88 λ q / D, D = illuminated mirror aperture, i.e. 0.44 λ/NA with NA = D/2q)² + (~2 × 2.355 × σ_slope × q)²]; demagnification p/q ~ 60 m / 0.07-0.15 m ~ 400-900; source FWHM = 2.355 σ (horizontal 35 µm APS-U vs 660 µm old). Use FDR results as anchors: 103 × 68 nm² (micro), 37 × 37 nm² (nano) at 14 keV (FWHM-like; RMS ~50 × 35 and ~19 × 19 nm, FDR Figs. 4.60-4.61); tolerance 0.4-0.75 nm rms figure error for <10% growth. Beam pointing: a lateral source shift dx moves the focus by dx q/p; an angular error dψ of the beam at the KB moves it by ~dψ × q.

interactiveIdeas.title: Flip the monochromator, keep the spot
interactiveIdeas.concept: Animated small-offset DCM: crystals slide in (single colour) and out (pink). A heater on crystal 2 slowly warms it; the exit beam tilts until the mono spot overlaps the pink spot on the sample.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: How thermal expansion of silicon is used as a micro-steering knob; why pink and mono must hit the same sub-micron volume.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: Si(111) d = 3.1356 Å; θ_B from 21.9° (5.3 keV) to 3.8° (30 keV). Heating crystal 2 by ΔT changes d by α ΔT (α_Si ~ 2.6 × 10⁻⁶ /K); Bragg angle mismatch Δθ = α ΔT tan(θ_B); exit-beam tilt 2 Δθ (~125 / 70 / 45 / 21 µrad at 5.3 / 9 / 14 / 30 keV for 60 K). Offset ~1.1 mm; closing it at the micro KB ~6 m downstream would need ~180 µrad, at the nano KB ~11.7 m downstream ~95 µrad. Horizontal-deflection polarization loss: PDR kinematic cos²(2θ) estimate ~1/2 at 5.3 keV, ~1/4 at 8 keV, ~10% at 12 keV; perfect-crystal (Darwin-width) scaling |cos 2θ| gives ~28% / ~12% / ~5%. dE/E ~ 1.3 × 10⁻⁴ for Si(111). Present the FDR wording ('intersects the pink beam at the sample') and flag the exact criterion as unconfirmed.

interactiveIdeas.title: Strain decoder: what moves a Laue spot?
interactiveIdeas.concept: Apply a rotation, a shear (deviatoric) strain, or a uniform expansion to a crystal and watch the Laue spots. Rotation moves all spots together; shear changes angles between spots; uniform expansion moves nothing - until you switch to the monochromator and see the energy shift.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: Laue patterns measure orientation and 5 of the 6 strain components; the 6th (volume change) needs one energy measurement; how this maps dislocation cells and residual stress in printed metals.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: Spot directions depend only on q-hat = q/|q|; a uniform dilatation scales all |q| without changing directions (invisible to Laue). Deviatoric strain ~10⁻⁴ resolution (best ~2 × 10⁻⁵). One 200 µm pixel at 510 mm is ~3.9 × 10⁻⁴ rad in 2θ, i.e. ~2 × 10⁻⁴ rad in the plane-normal direction (~2 × 10⁻⁴ in dd/d at 2θ = 90°); sub-pixel peak fitting over many reflections reaches 10⁻⁴ or better (the PDR's design rule of '1 pixel ~ 10⁻⁴' is a goal, not met exactly at 0.51 m). Rotations of 0.01° are easily visible. Full tensor = deviatoric (Laue) + dilatational (one reflection's energy, dE/E ~10⁻⁴).

funFacts: The 3DMN nano-focusing mirrors must match their ideal elliptical shape to within 0.4-0.5 nanometres rms - only a couple of atomic spacings - or the 40 nm spot blurs (FDR 2019).
A 10-cm piece of aluminium grows by 100 nm if it warms by just 0.04 °C, so the nano station sits in its own enclosure held to 0.02 °C (PDR 2017).

Using a sliding wire as a 'differential aperture' to get depth from a Laue pattern was introduced by the ORNL team of Larson, Yang, Ice, Budai and Tischler at the APS and published in Nature in 2002; it became the signature technique of 34-ID-E.

The old station's depth wire was a ~50 micrometre platinum wire hovering ~200 micrometres above the sample (34-ID-E 'End near focus' photo of the CCD-era, pre-2009 setup); 2022-23 geometry files use a 101.5 µm wire.
The gold 'barcode' coded aperture uses a de Bruijn sequence: in its 256 bits, every run of 8 bits appears exactly once - an idea borrowed from X-ray astronomy (Gursoy et al. 2022).

In 3DMN's monochromator the second silicon crystal is kept about 60 °C warmer than the first; silicon's thermal expansion then tilts the exit beam by roughly 0.02-0.13 milliradian (more at low energies), just enough to keep the single-colour and rainbow beams on the same spot (FDR).

Most of the Laue signal on the top detector comes from photons of about 12-17 keV: at lower energies few sets of atomic planes can reflect to 90 degrees, and at higher energies the reflections grow weak (PDR).
Before the upgrade, demand was so high that 34-ID-E proposals typically needed a review score of about 1.4 - closer to 'extraordinary' than 'excellent' - to get beam time (PDR).
As early as 2005, 34-ID-E demonstrated achromatic mirror focusing to 85 × 95 nm² at 15 keV (APS User Meeting poster, Liu et al.).
The design team estimated the upgrade could make some 3D experiments up to 45,000 times faster: ×100 brighter source, ×9 better mirrors, ×5 coded apertures, ×10 better detectors (PDR).
3DMN is expected to produce ~2.8 petabytes of raw data a year, about 7 times the pre-upgrade station (APS computing strategy 2024).
ATOMIC's X-ray beam travels straight through the 3DMN hutch inside a shielded pipe, so both beamlines can run while people work in 34-ID-E (FDR).
Before the upgrade 3DMN's predecessor used the inboard canted beam; after the upgrade 3DMN takes the outboard one (34-ID-E wiki vs FDR Table 4.62 / Fig. 4.59).

A 2026 study fed 3D wire-scan maps of a stainless-steel grain from 34-ID-E to an unsupervised machine-learning model to pick out dislocation cells at 0.5 micrometre depth resolution (SharafEldin et al.).

As-built focal sizes/flux: FDR ray traces give 103 × 68 nm² (micro) and 37 × 37 nm² (nano) at 14 keV; the Beamline Directory quotes 0.15 × 0.15 µm and 10¹⁴ (pink) / 10¹¹ (mono, 15 keV) ph/s; no commissioning measurement has been published. MEDSI 2025 states all feature beamlines met their KPPs but gives no 3DMN numbers. Note that APS-U feature-beamline KPPs were brightness at a defined energy and usable energy range (only ISN had a spot-size KPP), so meeting the KPP does not certify the 3DMN focal size.
Undulator length: FDR gives 2.1 m for both canted devices; the ATOMIC directory entry says its revolver is 2.3 m. As-built 3DMN U28 length not independently confirmed.

First-mirror cooling: PDR (2017) proposed LN2-cooled Si mirrors; FDR (2019) specifies flat 3-stripe Si mirrors at 3.0 mrad with a 'notch' anti-deformation design but no coolant. Deflection sense is no longer open in the design record: the PDR text and the FDR Fig. 4.59 schematic both show 3DMN deflecting outboard and ATOMIC inboard, consistent with the ~0.4 m separation in Fig. 4.58; as-built confirmation still welcome.

Mono heater criterion: the FDR says the heated second crystal tilts the mono beam so it 'intersects the pink beam at the sample position'; Pateras et al. (34-ID-C precursor) say it keeps the mono beam 'coincident to the pink beam in the final focusing optics' - these describe the same crossing point (KB ~0.1 m from the sample), so they do not conflict. The open issue is quantitative: 2·α·ΔT·tan(θ_B) at ΔT ~ 60 K gives ~20-125 µrad (30 → 5.3 keV), whereas closing a 1.1 mm offset at the micro KB (~6 m) needs ~180 µrad and at the nano KB (~11.7 m) ~95 µrad; and a crossing angle ψ at the KB shifts the focus by ~ψ × q (microns). How the as-built system keeps pink and mono on the same sub-100 nm spot (energy-dependent ΔT, KB re-alignment, residual offset) needs confirmation from beamline staff.

Hutch boundaries and widths are read from the FDR Fig. 4.58 scale bar (± ~0.3 m; widths rougher); 34-ID-D no longer appears in the FDR naming and appears to have been absorbed into the enlarged 34-ID-E.

Sample positions: FDR tabulates instrument/KB positions (60.0 m, 65.5 m); actual focal-plane positions depend on as-built focal lengths (PDR design 70/142 mm micro, 55/120 mm nano, working distance ≥ 50 / ~30 mm).

Depth-resolution hardware in routine use after the upgrade (Pt wire vs coded aperture/mask scans): coded apertures are demonstrated (2022-2025) and 'mask scan' reconstruction was 'R&D prototyping' in 2024; routine user availability not confirmed.
Whether undulator gap taper (supported up to 5 mm by the APS-U HPMU drive) is used to smooth the pink-beam spectrum for Laue after the upgrade.
Energy range: 5.3-30 keV (FDR, PDR) vs 5.5-30 keV (current directory).

Status: on 2026-10-05 3DMN was at stage 5 (scientific commissioning/early experiments); the date it enters the general user program (stage 6) is not announced, although 34-ID-E already appears on the GU proposal beamline list. Early 2D experiments ran ~late July 2026 and 3D (HPC-scale coded-aperture) experiments were planned 'in winter' (ModSim 2026 talk).

Minor FDR inconsistency for the partner beamline: ATOMIC KB1 at 52.0 m (Table 4.63) vs 'station C at 54 m' (text). Also the old 34-ID-E wiki says the canted beams are separated by '1 µrad' - an obvious typo for 1 mrad.

Pink-beam flux comparison: PDR says ~10¹⁴ ph/s pink is '~50×' current operations at 500 nm, while the 2016 web spec lists 10¹¹ ph/s (white) for the old station - the two pre-upgrade baselines are inconsistent.

Detector model naming: the pre-upgrade top panel is 'XRD 1621' in Das et al. 2018 and the lauelab geometry ID ('PE1621'), but 'XRD 1620 AN' in the 2024 computing strategy; the side panels are 'XRD 0820 AN' on the Instruments page/computing strategy but 'PE0822' in 2022-23 geometry files. Use the generic 'PerkinElmer 2k × 2k / 1k × 1k a-Si flat panels' unless staff confirm.
